difficultyRationale: Tests whether candidates distinguish a class's shared blueprint from an object's independent per-instance state, a baseline OOP distinction rather than a trick question.
explanation: Each `new Counter()` call allocates a distinct object with its own copy of the `value` field. The class is only the shared blueprint describing what fields and methods every Counter has; the field values themselves are per-object state, so c1 and c2 evolve independently.

options.text: 1 1 — because value is declared inside the class, Java treats it as shared state across every instance, similar to a static field.
options.explanation: This would only be true if value were declared static. As a plain instance field, each object gets its own copy, so increments on c1 cannot leak into c2.

options.text: 2 2 — once any Counter instance calls increment(), the change is reflected in every other instance of the same class, because the compiler treats every field declared inside a class body as implicitly shared across all objects created from that same blueprint unless a special per-instance keyword is used.
options.explanation: Instance fields are not automatically synchronized across objects; only a static field is shared at the class level. This answer describes static-field semantics, not the instance field actually declared here.

options.text: 2 1 — c1 and c2 are separate objects created from the same class blueprint, so each has its own independent copy of the value field; incrementing one does not affect the other.
options.explanation: Each `new Counter()` call allocates a distinct object with its own `value` field. The class only defines the shape shared by all instances; the state itself is per-object, so c1 ends at 2 and c2 ends at 1.

options.text: A compile error occurs because Counter does not declare a constructor, so new Counter() is invalid.
options.explanation: Java automatically supplies a public no-argument default constructor when a class declares none, so new Counter() compiles and runs without any constructor being written explicitly.
